source: Durian Orchard (ការដាំធូរេន), by Vann Thana Busab and Montry Vong Phanith, published by the Northwest Cambodia Provinces Fruit Culture Development Committee (Battambang), 1998, 59pp, AIDOC code 178-001
text:
The source's pest and disease section opens with a general principle: growers should inspect the orchard regularly and act as soon as a problem is first spotted on a small number of fruit or trees, rather than waiting until an infestation or infection has spread, since durian pest and disease problems are much harder and more costly to control once established across an orchard.

Fruit borer (a caterpillar/moth pest of developing fruit; the exact Khmer common-name string used by this specific source could not be transcribed with full confidence from the scan and is not repeated here to avoid shipping an unverified Khmer term -- see the Durian fruit borer entry in Source B of this batch for a confidently-sourced scientific name): a caterpillar pest that bores into the developing fruit, usually entering near the stalk end or where two fruit are touching, and feeds inside the flesh and seed area, leaving a visible entry hole often with frass (insect droppings/sawdust-like debris) around it. Damaged fruit should be removed from the tree and destroyed (not left on the ground nearby) to reduce the population feeding on the next fruit set, and growers are advised to keep developing fruit from touching one another (part of the reasoning behind the thinning schedule above) since the borer moths favor laying eggs where fruit surfaces are in contact.

The source's coverage of insect pests beyond the fruit borer, and of the specific fungal diseases affecting stems, roots, and fruit, is present in the source but the scanned image resolution available for this batch was not always sufficient to transcribe pesticide names, dosages, and fine symptom detail with full confidence; growers should cross-reference the more detailed pest/disease entries from Source B and Source C in this same batch, which cover durian stem canker, root rot, pink disease, leaf blight, and several insect pests with genus/species names.
